title: The Vow of Sandpiper Point
premise: Kestrel Galloway, a ghostwriter who hides behind other people's names, is hired to write the memoirs of orchard magnate Delphine Marsh — only to discover the deed to her beloved Sandpiper Point orchard lists two estranged co-owners: Delphine and the sister she hasn't spoken to in thirty years, Ione. As Kestrel shuttles between the sisters, transcribing their competing truths, he falls for the town's ferry operator, Wren, whose own loyalty to one sister threatens everything he's documenting. When a developer's deadline forces the sale of the orchard, Kestrel must choose between publishing the memoir that will make his career and forging a third document — a new deed — that gives both women a way back to each other. In the end he lets his own name be erased from the byline, keeps Wren past the last train of the season, and watches the sisters sign together as the first frost settles on the trees.
about_author: Vesper Okafor is the pen name of a former court stenographer who spent a decade listening to other people's confessions before writing her own fiction. She lives on a tidal inlet where the ferries stop running each November, which she insists is the best month for telling the truth.

chapters.title: The Ghost in the Margins
chapters.summary: Kestrel Galloway, POV. A ghostwriter who has never used his own name on a book, Kestrel accepts a lucrative commission from publisher Aldous Vane: the memoirs of orchard matriarch Delphine Marsh at Sandpiper Point. The emotional beat is restless ambition — Kestrel believes second chances belong to people with better timing, and this book could finally buy him a name of his own.

chapters.title: Two Names on One Deed
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV. Reviewing estate papers in Delphine's drafty farmhouse, Kestrel finds the orchard deed lists two owners: Delphine and 'Ione Marsh,' a name Delphine refuses to say aloud. When pressed, she only says, 'She knows what she did.' The beat is intrigue laced with dread — Kestrel senses the memoir's real story is the one he's been told not to write.

chapters.title: The Ferry That Stops in November
chapters.summary: Wren Okonkwo, POV. Ferry operator Wren ferries Kestrel across the sound to Sandpiper Point and pegs him instantly as an outsider who takes notes about people instead of talking to them. Their banter crackles; Wren warns him the last train of the season leaves in six weeks. The beat is reluctant attraction — two people fluent in leaving.

chapters.title: What Delphine Remembers
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV. First recorded interview sessions: Delphine recounts founding the orchard with her sister, then a fire, a betrayal over inheritance, and thirty years of silence. Her version is polished, rehearsed, almost too perfect. Kestrel notices gaps shaped like guilt. The beat is seduction of narrative — a beautiful story that may be a beautiful lie.

chapters.title: The Woman Across the Sound
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Wren reveals she knows Ione Marsh — she runs supplies to the small island cottage where Ione lives alone, tending a mirror orchard of scraggly trees. Wren's loyalty to Ione is fierce and unexplained. She makes Kestrel promise not to ambush the old woman. The beat is divided allegiance foreshadowed.

chapters.title: Interview with a Stranger
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV. Under pretense of a land survey, Kestrel meets Ione, who sees through him in minutes but talks anyway — offering a rawer, harsher version of the fire and the betrayal. Her account contradicts Delphine's in every detail that matters. The beat is vertigo: Kestrel realizes whichever truth he writes will destroy someone.

chapters.title: Draft One, Lies Included
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV. Writing Delphine's chapters at night, Kestrel smooths contradictions into something publishable and hates how easily it comes. He sends pages to Vane, who loves them. Wren reads over his shoulder and goes quiet. The beat is complicity — the first time Kestrel chooses craft over truth and feels it cost him something with her.

chapters.title: The Developer's Letter
chapters.summary: Delphine, POV. A development consortium offers Delphine a fortune for Sandpiper Point, contingent on clear title — meaning Ione must sign away her half or be bought out by court order within weeks. Delphine drafts a letter demanding Ione sell, then can't send it. The beat is pride at war with grief; the deadline becomes the novel's ticking clock.

chapters.title: Apples After Frost
chapters.summary: Kestrel and Wren, alternating. Walking the orchard after the first frost, Kestrel and Wren grow close; she shows him the grafting shed where the sisters' childhood initials are carved side by side. He tells her, haltingly, about the years he spent invisible under other writers' names. The beat is intimacy — the first time either says something true without notes.

chapters.title: Ione Comes to Town
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Ione crosses the sound unannounced to see the orchard one last time before the developers move, and nearly runs into Delphine at the farm gate. Thirty years collapse into one vicious exchange about the fire. Wren shields Ione, cementing her side. The beat is rupture — the wound reopened, witnessed by the man hired to heal it into prose.

chapters.title: The Chapter Vane Won't Buy
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV. Kestrel writes the true version — both sisters' accounts braided together — and sends it to Vane, who rejects it as unsellable and threatens to give the book to another writer unless Kestrel delivers Delphine's story, clean and flattering, in ten days. The beat is the squeeze: his name, his escape, priced against two old women's truth.

chapters.title: What Actually Burned
chapters.summary: Ione, POV. Ione finally tells Wren (and, overhearing, Kestrel) the full truth: the fire was set by their father to void the joint deed and disinherit Ione; Delphine stayed silent to keep the land, believing Ione had betrayed her first with a secret sale offer. The beat is tragic revelation — both sisters wrong, both loyal, both too proud to ask.

chapters.title: Ten Days
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV. Kestrel tries to write the false memoir and cannot. He burns through nights drafting three versions, destroying each. Wren, learning he still intends to finish Vane's book, asks him directly whose side he's on; he has no answer. The beat is the dark middle — identity crisis made literal on the page.

chapters.title: The Last Train Schedule
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Wren posts the final ferry-and-train schedule of the season: November 30th, then nothing until spring. She and Kestrel circle what happens after — whether he stays, whether she'd ask. Neither commits. The beat is tender avoidance; love measured against departure times.

chapters.title: Delphine Reads Herself
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV. Desperate, Kestrel breaks his contract's spirit and lets Delphine read the braided true manuscript. She reads all night; in the morning she admits she knew the fire was her father's doing — and let Ione take the blame because losing her sister felt survivable and losing the orchard didn't. The beat is confession, earned at last.

chapters.title: A Third Document
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV. Kestrel conceives the impossible fix: not a memoir, not a sale, but a new deed — a covenant reuniting the sisters' halves and protecting the orchard from development, drafted in language neither woman can hide behind. He'll need both signatures, Vane's manuscript killed, and his fee forfeited. The beat is resolve; the ghostwriter decides to author something real.

chapters.title: Vane's Ultimatum
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV. Vane arrives in person, offers double the advance for the flattering version and blacklisting if Kestrel walks. Kestrel hands back the advance check and every page of the false draft. Vane promises to bury him. The beat is sacrifice — Kestrel torches the career he built invisibility to protect.

chapters.title: Crossing the Sound
chapters.summary: Wren and Kestrel, alternating. On the last week of service, Wren carries Delphine across the water herself — the first time in thirty years — while Kestrel brings Ione to the mainland dock. The sisters meet on the water, between shores, neither on home ground. The beat is trembling reconciliation; the deed waits on the table between them.

chapters.title: Signatures
chapters.summary: Ensemble, anchored on Kestrel. In the farmhouse kitchen, Delphine and Ione argue, weep, and finally sign the covenant deed side by side beneath the carved initials in the grafting shed. The developer's option dies; the orchard holds. The beat is catharsis — justice achieved entirely outside any courtroom, by two pens and one stubborn document.

chapters.title: The Byline
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV. Vane publishes the memoir anyway from stolen drafts, credited to a house writer; Kestrel's name appears nowhere, exactly as he lived. But Ione asks him to write their true story properly, and Delphine agrees to sign whatever he writes. The beat is quiet vindication — invisibility chosen rather than imposed.

chapters.title: After the Last Train
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. November 30th: the final ferry crossing, the last train's whistle down the coast. Kestrel stands on the dock with a packed bag and doesn't board. Wren ties off the boat for winter. The beat is the vow kept — someone stays after the last train leaves, and it's him.

chapters.title: First Frost, Second Chances
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV, epilogue. Spring: pruning season at Sandpiper Point. Kestrel writes at the farmhouse table under his own name for the first time, the sisters bickering over grafting technique, Wren arriving on the morning boat. The beat is arrival — a man who believed timing was destiny learns that staying is a choice you make daily.
